title: The Gain-Loss Ratio: Defining a Missing Quantity in Human Capacity Dynamics
content: A three-week detraining study can leave slow loss indistinguishable from none, and a freely fitted decay curve cannot tell whether a flat line means nothing was lost or nothing was there to lose. This paper defines the within-person gain-loss ratio, \(R = k_g/k_l\), from train-then-detrain rate constants, with a bounded form, \(\Phi = k_g/(k_g + k_l)\), and derives what each design can identify. Both are invariant to units and baseline; quotients of averaged rates also depend on amplitudes and windows. Retention inference requires justified information about the decay end level or amplitude, and a baseline anchor below a retained end level biases the loss rate downward by a computable multiple of the share retained. With a fitted end level, the loss rate's relative error grows as the inverse square of rate times window. A closed-form three-point sampling design is optimal; in a representative case it needs about half the visits of equal spacing. Under training on a fraction \(D\) of days, in the fast-cycling limit the mean share above the resting level is \(DR/(DR + 1 - D)\); for weekly cycles, an exact solution and a theorem show that equal training-rest pairs keep the lowest level highest. A difference identity tests whether one exponential suffices. With unknown outcome scale, one averaged training frequency cannot identify \(R\); two informative fractions can. Falsification criteria are stated as variance components with exact power. On published data, the ratio is computable in the hypertrophic domain but not yet in the neural one.
